title: Job contracting vs labor-only contracting
primary_topics: Plain-language explanation of the legal distinction between permissible job contracting and prohibited labor-only contracting
DO 174 (2017) as the current regulatory framework for contractualization
Sasan vs NLRC (2008) as the definitive Supreme Court test for legitimate job contracting
sub_topics: Simple residential-house analogy: owner (principal), contractor with sufficient capital
DO 174 Series 2017: 'sufficient capital' = paid-up capital or net worth of at least P5 million
Job contracting: contractor supplies labor, materials, equipment, pays workers -- workers are contractor's employees
Owner's solidary liability only if contractor underpays workers
Labor-only contracting triggers: contractor recruits only, OR owner pays salaries, OR owner supervises, OR owner provides equipment
Labor Code Art. 106 prohibition of labor-only contracting
Supply of construction materials by owner does not convert job contracting to labor-only
Subcontracting: cleaning, guarding, medical clinic -- each a separate job contract if properly capitalized and controlled
Outsourcing as the Digital Age synonym for job contracting
Sasan vs NLRC (Oct. 17, 2008): three-part test for legitimate job contracting
Sasan test: (a) independent business + own responsibility + own manner; (b) substantial capital/investment; (c) contractual employees entitled to all labor and safety standards
Labor-only contracting elements: (a) no substantial capital; (b) employees perform activities directly related to principal's main business

directly related to the main business of the principal

stances.claim: Job contracting (outsourcing) is legally permissible and distinct from prohibited labor-only contracting: the key determinants are whether the contractor has substantial capital/investment, exercises control over workers, and assures them all labor standards — not whether the owner supplies some materials.
stances.rhetorical_move: legal-clarity advocacy: plain-language exposition to demystify a politically charged issue and separate legitimate from prohibited practices

stances.claim: The three triggers for prohibited labor-only contracting — contractor recruits only, owner pays salaries, or owner supervises or provides equipment — are the operative tests, not the size or formality of the arrangement.
stances.rhetorical_move: trigger-identification as practical guidance for principals and contractors navigating DO 174

notable_anecdotes: The residential-house construction analogy — a homeowner hiring a P5-million-capitalized contractor to build a house, then exploring what changes when the contractor subcontracts cleaning, guarding, and a medical clinic — used as a two-step pedagogic escalator from simple to complex contractualization scenarios without any legal jargon in the first pass.

The aside that 'outsourcing is the digital-age synonym of job contracting' — connecting a vintage legal term to its contemporary business usage, bridging the gap between the Labor Code's language and the lived vocabulary of the modern economy.

The supply-of-materials clarification: an owner providing cement, gravel, and wood to the contractor does not convert legitimate job contracting into prohibited labor-only contracting — a common misconception explicitly addressed to prevent misapplication of the distinction.

Workers and unions seeking to understand their rights under job contracting arrangements
Lawyers advising principals and contractors on DO 174 compliance
Law students studying labor law and the Sasan doctrine
General civic readership following the contractualization policy debate

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban provides a plain-language explanation of the contractualization debate by walking through two escalating hypotheticals. In the simple version, a homeowner hires a properly capitalized contractor (DO 174: at least P5M paid-up capital or net worth) to build a house; the contractor supplies labor, materials, and equipment, pays workers at least minimum wage, and the homeowner is not the employer -- this is permissible job contracting under Labor Code Art. 106. Labor-only contracting (prohibited) arises if the contractor merely recruits workers while the owner pays salaries, supervises work, or provides equipment. In the complex version, a contractor for a P5-billion multi-building project subcontracts cleaning, security, and medical services to three separately capitalized entities -- each is still legitimate job contracting because the subcontractors control, pay, and equip their own workers. He anchors the analysis in Sasan vs NLRC (October 17, 2008), which sets a three-part test: (a) the contractor carries on an independent business in its own manner and under its own responsibility; (b) has substantial capital or investment; and (c) assures contractual employees full labor and safety standards -- contrasted with the two labor-only contracting elements: no substantial capital, and employees performing activities directly related to the principal's main business. He closes by noting that 'outsourcing is the digital-age synonym of job contracting.'
